# The Ocean of Auspicious Times
<note>original: "Muhurtasindhu"</note>

The line that originates from the base of the little finger <term>kanishthika</term><note>the pinky finger</note> and moves toward the space between the forefinger <term>pradeshini</term> and the middle finger indicates the span of one's life. If the line is full and long, life is long; if it is short or broken, the lifespan is diminished. (13) At the base of the thumb are the lines of progeny. Large, thick lines indicate sons, while thin, fine lines indicate daughters. Lines that are unbroken and long signify children with long lives, while broken or short lines signify those with short lives. (14)

Thus have been described the auspicious signs of women. Those that are the opposite are considered inauspicious. I shall now summarize those traits which are particularly fruitless or negative. (15) If a woman’s ring finger <note>the finger next to the little finger</note> does not touch the ground when she walks, or if her forefinger exceeds the length of her thumb, she is considered to be of a crooked or sinful nature. (16)

Those with dry, hairless, or excessively fleshy shanks <note>the lower leg</note>, or those with two whorls of hair on the head, or a depressed and small pubic area, or a belly shaped like a pot <note>protruding or distended</note>, are destined for a life of sorrow. (17) A very short neck leads to extreme poverty, while an excessively long neck indicates the destruction of one's lineage. A woman with a very broad neck is said to possess a fierce or violent temperament. (18)

She whose eyes are squinted or tawny-colored <note>yellowish-brown</note>, or whose gaze is dark and unsteady, is of bad character. Those who have deep dimples in their cheeks when they smile are certainly said to be unchaste. (19) A woman with a high or protruding forehead is said to bring harm to her husband's younger brother; if the nape of the neck is protruding, she harms her father-in-law; and if the buttocks are excessively hairy, she harms her husband. A woman with a very hairy upper lip is not auspicious for her husband, nor is one who is excessively tall. (20)

Breasts that are hairy or discolored, and ears that are uneven, bring distress. Teeth that are thick, jagged, or uneven, or gums that are blackish in color, indicate a life of hardship or a tendency toward theft. (21) Women whose hands bear marks resembling carnivorous animals—such as wolves, crows, vultures, serpents, or owls—or whose hands are dry, veiny, and irregular, will be devoid of happiness and wealth. (22)

She who has a raised upper lip and rough hair is fond of quarreling. Generally, defects are found in those who are unattractive, for it is said: "Where there is beauty, there the virtues reside." (23)

<note>The following section describes the division of the body into parts for astrological or divinatory mapping.</note>

The feet including the ankles are designated as the first part. The shanks and the knees are the second. The private parts and the scrotum <note>referring here to the general pelvic region in the context of the human form</note> are the third. The navel and the waist are called the fourth. (24) The abdomen is said to be the fifth. The heart and the breasts are the sixth. The shoulders and the collarbones <term>ansajatruni</term> are called the seventh and eighth.

## On the Consideration of the Jackal's Cry
<note>original: "Shiva-svara-vichara"; Shiva here refers to the female jackal, often used in divination.</note>

Jackals are similar to dogs in the results they portend. Their specific distinction is that they are intoxicated with passion during the winter season. The sounds "Hoo-Hoo" at the end, and "Ta-Ta" thereafter, are called "Full Tones" <term>Purna-svara: sounds indicating fulfillment or success</term>, while others are described as "Blazing" <term>Pradipta: sounds indicating danger or intensity</term>. 1.

Indeed, the "Kak-ha" sound of the female jackal arises from her full nature. Any other sounds she makes that depart from her natural disposition are all declared by the tradition to be "Blazing" <note>inauspicious or alarming</note>. 2.

A jackal howling in the East or the North is peaceful and honored everywhere. However, if she faces the "Smoky" direction <note>the direction where the sun is currently located</note>, she destroys the lords of the directions with her blazing voice. 3.

A blazing cry is auspicious in all directions, and especially excellent at the beginning of the day. But in a city or an army, if the jackal is on the left side and facing the sun, it forebodes great distress. 4.

The cry "Yahi" <note>Go!</note> commands fear; "Ta-Ta" is the herald of death; and the "Dhir-Ghu-Hoo" sound is said to be "Flaming," signifying the destruction of the country. 5.

Some claim there is no harshness in a jackal on the right side. Because of the moisture in her mouth, she acts like an actor under the sun's rays. 6.

Now, if she is obstructed in the South, she foretells a certain death. That same jackal, howling in the West, foretells a death in the water. 7.

Steadfastness, hearing [good news], the acquisition of wealth, the arrival of money, the distinction of chief officials, and the prosperity of vehicles— 8. —these results are given within a month if the cry is heard in these directions. In the South, the result is the opposite, occurring in six or five months. 9.

That jackal which causes horripilation <note>goosebumps</note> in men, or causes horses to void dung and urine, and creates terror by her howling—she is not "Shiva" <note>Auspicious</note>; she brings no good. 10.

The jackal that remains silent when challenged by the cry of a master, or by the sound of men, elephants, or horses, bestows auspiciousness upon the army or the city. 11.

The jackal crying "Bhe-Bhe" is a bringer of fear; "Bho-Bho" indicates calamity and announces the death of a kinsman. The sounds "Phi-Pha" and "Hoo-Hoo" are also included in the jackal's vocalizations. 12.

They carry the highest sounds from the peaceful syllable... <note>The text here contains numerical notations 8|8 likely referring to a specific classification</note> ...or the dark one. The sound "Te-Te" first and "The-The" afterwards is a cry born of satisfaction. 13.

Having first uttered a loud and terrible syllable, the jackal then cries "Ko-She"...

# The Ocean of Auspicious Moments
<note>Original: Muhūrtasindhu. This title is used interchangeably with Muhūrtaratnākara (The Jewel-Mine of Auspicious Moments) in this manuscript.</note>

...the path is safe; he spoke of the great union of bile <note>likely a medical or physiological reference in the context of omens</note> with the beloved woman. (54) **Thus ends the section on the cries of birds at night.**

### On the Cry of the Owl
When the owl cries "Hūm-Hūm" or "Gugguli" with joy, desiring its mate, it is considered "Full" <note>Pūrṇa: a technical term for a favorable direction or timing in divination</note>. The sound "Lulu-Sadi" is also always to be known as favorable. The sound "Kim-Kim" signifies a quarrel. If it repeatedly cries "Vala-Vala," it brings misfortune. The sounds "Tata-Tata" are likewise not auspicious; the rest are considered "Blazing" <note>Pradīpta: an astrological term for harsh or unfavorable omens</note>.

Now, if an owl hoots atop someone's house during the day or night, it portends the death of the master of the house, or the loss of children and livestock. If it hoots over the cowshed, it means the loss of cattle; if over the granary, the loss of grains. Therefore, one should perform the "Peace Rituals" <note>Shanti: rites performed to avert evil</note> as prescribed in the ritual manuals.

The same applies to other portents. Because of the shifting nature of time, this compendium named **The Jewel-Mine of Auspicious Moments** (Muhūrtaratnākara) has been diligently composed for the wise. It consists of sixteen "Waves" <note>Kallolas: the author uses the metaphor of a sea (Sindhu) divided into waves rather than chapters</note> and is dedicated to the feet of the yellow-robed Lord <note>Vishnu</note>. (1)

The chapters are as follows:
1. Considerations of Time
2. Auspicious Moments (Muhūrta)
3. Solar Transits (Sankrānti)
4. Planetary Transits (Gocara)
5. Sacraments (Samskāra)
6. Marriage (Parinayana)
7. Compatibility (Vadhūveśaka)
8. The Return of the Bride (Dvirāgamana)
9. Royal Consecration (Abhiṣeka)
10. Architecture (Vāstu)
11. Entry (Praveśa)
12. Miscellaneous (Miśra)
13. Primary Matters (Prathama)
14. Diverse Topics (Sankīrṇa)
...making sixteen in total. (4)

Having seen the works composed by the ancient sages such as Raibhya and others, this concise compendium was made for the benefit of the people. (5) This work was commissioned by the illustrious **Meharachandra**, a promoter of knowledge, in the year **1804** <note>Vikrama Samvat, roughly 1747-1748 CE</note> during the bright fortnight, on the thirteenth day of the dark half of the month under the autumn season. It reached completion through my service to the Holy Teacher.

If there are errors due to confusion or limited intellect, may the scholars set aside envy and refine this work after due consideration. Through service to my father's lotus-feet, my intellect became bright; I have created this entire work with devotion, like a sun to the darkness of ignorance.

**Thus ends the sixteenth wave in the "Jewel-Mine of Auspicious Moments" commissioned by Meharachandra, born of the illustrious Vāḍava lineage.** (16)

May there be auspiciousness! May this work expand by the grace of the Mother of the World. By the praise of the Divine, I bow to the Son of Nanda <note>Krishna</note>. May all be auspicious for the student and the reader. Note that the first half was written in four parts and the second half in two, proceeding in a circular order. (6)
